bib.title: Chapter 5. Cognitive Architectures with LangGraph (Learning LangChain)

question: How should the LLM application components (prompting, RAG, memory) be assembled, and how does the choice trade agency against reliability?
contributions: Classifies LLM application recipes (cognitive architectures 0 to 3 in the text) by which of three decisions the LLM makes
Shows LLM call, chain and router architectures implemented as LangGraph StateGraphs

results.claim: The chapter names the key trade-off in LLM apps as agency versus reliability, with an email assistant as the running example.
results.setup: Hypothetical email assistant that archives, replies or marks for review
results.quote: This hints at the key trade-off often faced when building LLM apps: the trade-off between agency (or the capacity to act autonomously) and relia‐
results.note: The summary calls it agency versus oversight

results.claim: The text-to-SQL chain uses temperature 0.1 for SQL generation and 0.7 for the explanation.
results.setup: Two ChatOpenAI instances, model_low_temp and model_high_temp, in the chain and router examples; model name not stated
results.note: The router example reuses the comment 'useful to generate SQL query' for the low-temperature model

limits: Chapter text defines only architectures 0 to 3 (code, LLM call, chain, router); agentic architectures are deferred to later chapters, though Figure 5-1 (image) also lists 4 state machine and 5 autonomous.
No evaluation or measurement of any architecture; examples are illustrative, with empty vector stores and no printed answers.
Router label is a free-text LLM output; the Literal type hint is not enforced at runtime and any non-'records' value routes to insurance.
Code is version-specific LangGraph and LangChain; JavaScript listings are truncated in the extracted text.
practices: List the constraints on the application first, since they inform the choice of architecture (Intro, email assistant).
Judge autonomy by how much an LLM decides: a step's output, the next step, or the available steps (Intro).
Use an LLM router to pick one index per query so irrelevant information stays out of the prompt (Architecture #3).
Use a lower temperature for SQL generation and a higher one for natural-language output (Architecture #2 code).
Use separate input and output schemas on the StateGraph to control what the caller supplies and receives; internal keys still appear in stream() output (Architecture #2).
An LLM can act as the query classifier with zero or very few examples, replacing a trained classifier (Architecture #3 note).
